Necrophilia is a noun that refers to a sexual attraction to, or sexual activity with, dead bodies (corpses).

Necrophilia describes when a person is sexually aroused by or engages in sexual acts with a dead human body. The word is used in two overlapping ways:

  • As a behavior — the act of engaging in sexual contact with a corpse.
  • As a psychological condition — an abnormal sexual attraction toward dead bodies, even without acting on it.

Both meanings are captured under the same word, so context usually tells you which one is meant.

In psychology, necrophilia is classified as a paraphilia — a term for an unusual or atypical pattern of sexual attraction. Most paraphilias involve attraction to things, situations, or (in more serious cases) beings that are not capable of consenting to a sexual encounter. Necrophilia falls firmly in this category because a dead person cannot, by definition, give consent or experience anything at all.

It is not merely considered unusual or taboo; it is considered a serious psychological disorder because:

  1. The object of desire is not a living person. Healthy human sexuality is oriented toward living partners capable of mutual participation.
  2. It often accompanies other psychological issues. In documented cases, necrophilia has been associated with extreme social withdrawal, antisocial personality traits, or other severe mental health conditions — though it can, rarely, occur in people who otherwise appear to function normally.
  3. It fundamentally violates human dignity. Even after death, a person's body is generally regarded, both legally and ethically, as deserving respect.

Psychologists and researchers have noted that necrophilia is not a single, uniform condition. It exists on a spectrum:

  • Necrophilic fantasy — a person is aroused by thoughts or fantasies involving dead bodies but never acts on them.
  • Necrophilic behavior — a person actually engages in sexual contact with a corpse. This is the rarer and more serious form and is what most people mean when they use the word.
  • Romantic necrophilia — in some documented cases, a person develops an intense emotional or romantic attachment to the dead (sometimes a deceased partner), which may or may not include a sexual component.

It is worth noting that reported cases of necrophilia have, in some instances, involved people who worked in settings where they had access to dead bodies — such as mortuaries, hospitals, or forensic facilities. This does not mean such professionals are necrophiliac; the overwhelming majority are not. It simply explains why some cases come to light in those professional contexts.

In most countries and jurisdictions, necrophilia is illegal. Laws against it are typically framed around:

  • Desecration or abuse of a corpse — treating a dead body in a disrespectful or unlawful manner.
  • Violation of burial and mortuary laws — interfering with a body that is under legal custody (such as in a morgue or cemetery).

The exact legal framing differs by country, but the act is criminalized nearly universally because societies recognize that human remains deserve protection from violation, and that allowing such acts would cause deep harm to the dignity of the deceased and the grief of their families.

• Necrophilia vs. necromancy — These sound similar but mean entirely different things. Necromancy is the (fictional or ritualistic) practice of communicating with the dead or summoning spirits — it belongs to mythology, folklore, and fantasy. It has no sexual meaning.
  • Necrophilia vs. thanatophilia — Thanatophilia is sometimes used as a synonym for necrophilia, but it can also refer more broadly to an obsessive fascination with death in general (not necessarily sexual). Necrophilia is the more precise, clinical term for the sexual aspect.

Outside of clinical, legal, or academic writing, the word necrophilia is rarely used in casual conversation. When it does appear, it is almost always in:

  • Medical or psychological literature — as a clinical diagnosis or case study term.
  • Legal documents or news reports — when discussing a crime involving a corpse.
  • Cultural criticism or dark humor — sometimes used metaphorically (and loosely) to describe an obsession with things that are old, dead, or past — though this metaphorical use is informal and imprecise.

Necrophilia is a sexual attraction to or sexual activity with dead human bodies — it is classified as a psychological disorder, is almost universally illegal, and is considered a serious violation of human dignity.
